cf.title: Convert ALL SubLinks to ANY SubLinks

input.subject: Convert ALL SubLinks to ANY SubLinks

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and the rewrite reuses the existing ANY sublink code in one planner file. Three fixable points remain. standards-compat-1 is a reproducible error in v2 for a valid operator class (message #8). standards-compat-2 is the unmeasured risk of worse plans after pull-up. already-exists-1 notes that NOT IN already gives the hashed SubPlan for `<> ALL`, and the thread has no benchmark.

brief.title: Planner rewrites ALL sublinks as negated ANY sublinks
brief.problem: The planner runs ALL sublinks as a nested-loop SubPlan, and they get none of the ANY sublink optimizations: hashed SubPlans and pull-up into semijoins or anti-joins. Queries using `<> ALL` (a common way to write NOT IN semantics) or other `op ALL` forms pay for this.
brief.proposed_design: In prepjointree.c the planner replaces each operator with its negator and applies De Morgan's laws: `foo op ALL (sub)` becomes `NOT (foo negator_op ANY (sub))`, and `NOT (foo op ALL (sub))` becomes `foo negator_op ANY (sub)`. The rewritten sublink then uses hashing or pull-up when it qualifies. If an operator has no negator, the ALL sublink stays unchanged.
user_visible_surface: Plan shapes change: ALL sublinks can appear as hashed ANY SubPlans, semijoins or anti-joins in EXPLAIN output.
author_claims: Converted sublinks can use hashed SubPlans and can be flattened into semijoins or anti-joins.
Worst case is a nested-loop ANY SubPlan with the same performance as today, so there are no regressions.
The negated ANY subplan stops on the same inner tuple as the ALL subplan; the only cost added is one NOT per outer tuple.
Join-order problems after pull-up belong to the join search and are handled with join_collapse_limit and geqo_threshold.
brief.thread_state: Lepikhov disputes the no-regression claim, citing larger join problems and LATERAL limits after pull-up; solai v tested v2 and gave +1. Rui Zhao found that v2 errors for a valid custom operator class whose negator is outside the opfamily, and posted a fix that Richard has not yet answered.
unclear: The material gives no benchmark numbers for any case.
Richard has not said whether he accepts Rui's op_in_opfamily() check or prefers one of the other two fixes.
The material does not say how the patch checks that NULL semantics are kept, beyond solai's manual tests.
Nobody addresses the join_collapse_limit regressions Lepikhov raised, beyond advising users to tune settings.
The material does not say whether non-btree operators or commutated row comparisons were checked for opfamily consistency.

prior_attempts.title: Convert NOT IN to anti-joins when possible
prior_attempts.quote:
It has been close to three months since this last update, so marked
the patch as returned with feedback.
prior_attempts.reason: Antonin Houska showed that join quals used as not-null proofs can be wrong when the NOT IN is in a JOIN/ON clause, because join order may let NULLs reach the anti-join. David Rowley limited the optimisation to WHERE-clause quals, and Antonin then sent review comments on that version. The author said he had no time to respond, and the entry was returned with feedback after about three months with no update.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P7 converted NOT IN to an anti-join with its own not-null proofs. This patch only rewrites ALL to a negated ANY and leaves pull-up to the existing and pending ANY rules.

prior_attempts.title: NOT IN to ANTI JOIN transformation
prior_attempts.reason: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown message is a rebased patch from June 2019, and no later reply appears before the April 2020 decision. Earlier, David Rowley noted that the added OR ... IS NULL join clauses force a nested loop join, and moved his competing patch to a separate thread.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P4 added OR ... IS NULL join clauses to handle nullable columns. This patch adds no NULL handling of its own and depends on the ANY and NOT ANY pull-up rules.

prior_attempts.title: Pull up sublink of type 'NOT NOT (expr)'
prior_attempts.quote: So I'm inclined to reject this patch as probably being a net loss in almost all cases. If you can show any real-world cases where it wins, we could reconsider.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane argued that pull_up_sublinks runs before transformations that could create NOT NOT, so it only sees NOT NOT that a user wrote by hand, and no one showed that this happens in real queries. Without such evidence the extra code and planning cycles would be a net loss for everyone else. Running expression simplification before pullup would need a second simplification pass, which he judged not worth the cost. The author agreed and asked for the patch to be rejected.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 removed hand-written NOT NOT, which is rare in real queries. `<> ALL` is standard syntax, and the rewrite runs only when an ALL sublink is present, so the net-loss reason applies less.

objections.title: The main case, <> ALL, already has a hashed path via NOT IN
objections.failure_scenario: A user who writes `x <> ALL (select ...)` can write `x NOT IN (select ...)` today with identical semantics, NULLs included, and already gets a hashed SubPlan. The patch adds a permanent planner rewrite whose main gain is a spelling that users can already change. Users of the other operators, such as `< ALL`, get help, but the proposal does not show that such users exist.
objections.argument: `NOT IN` is parsed as `NOT (x = ANY (...))`, which is the same tree this patch builds for `<> ALL`, so hashing for that form exists already. Pull-up into anti-joins depends on the separate NOT ANY patch noted in message #1, and that patch would cover NOT IN as well. The motivation in message #1 comes from a paper, and no field report of slow `op ALL` queries appears in the thread. [P2] rejected a pull_up_sublinks rewrite of hand-written forms because no real-world wins were shown.
objections.author_must_show: Which real queries, for example from ORMs or query generators, use `op ALL` forms that users cannot rewrite as NOT IN, and how much faster do they run?

precedents.title: Pull up sublink of type 'NOT NOT (expr)'

critic.reasoning: NOT IN does parse to the tree this patch builds for `<> ALL`, and the thread shows no user report or benchmark for other `op ALL` forms. [P2] is weak support, because `<> ALL` is a standard spelling, unlike hand-written NOT NOT.

objections.title: Rewrite turns valid row-comparison ALL queries into errors
objections.failure_scenario: A user has a btree operator class that passes amvalidate() but whose operator's NEGATOR is outside the family. After upgrade, a row-wise `op ALL` query that returned rows on master fails with "operator ... is not a member of opfamily". The user finds out when the query runs in production.
objections.argument: Message #8 shows the rewrite swaps in the negators but keeps the original rcexpr->opfamilies, so the result can be an inconsistent RowCompareExpr. The rewrite assumes a contract, that a NEGATOR is always a member of the same family, which Postgres does not enforce for user-defined operators. Rui posted three possible fixes, and the author has not yet chosen one. The brief also says non-btree operators and commutated row comparisons were not checked.
objections.author_must_show: Which conditions on negator and opfamily membership does the rewrite require, and does the patch check each of them before rewriting?

critic.reasoning: Message #8 gives a reproducible case where v2 turns a working query into an error. A fix is posted, but the author has not adopted one, and non-btree and commutated cases are unchecked.

objections.title: Existing ALL queries change plan shape with no opt-out
objections.failure_scenario: An application written with `<> ALL` runs a tuned plan today. After upgrade, pull-up merges the subquery into the outer join problem, and the join count goes past join_collapse_limit or picks up LATERAL limits. The query slows down, and the only remedies are raising limits or rewriting generated SQL.
objections.argument: Message #2 and message #5 report that new sublink pull-ups often cause user complaints for this reason. Message #3 answers that the join search is at fault and users should tune join_collapse_limit, but that is a workaround for users, not a design answer. The proposal shows no benchmark and offers no per-query or per-session way to keep today's ALL SubPlan behaviour.
objections.author_must_show: What can a user do, short of rewriting the query or raising join_collapse_limit, when the pulled-up ALL sublink gives a worse plan than before?

critic.reasoning: Lepikhov's concern in messages #2 and #5 is concrete, and the thread answers it only with advice to tune settings. The lack of an opt-out matches existing ANY pull-up, so the open point is the unmeasured regression risk for existing ALL queries.

refuted.title: Anti-join pull-up of rewritten <> ALL needs a shown NULL proof
refuted.failure_scenario: A user writes `x <> all (select y ...)` inside the ON clause of a join, where outer-join order can let NULLs reach the anti-join. The planner rewrites it to `not (x = any ...)` and pulls it up into an anti-join. Rows that should be filtered out are returned, and nobody notices until a report differs from an older release.
refuted.argument: Message #7 reports that v2 turns ALL sublinks into anti-joins, and message #1 says this relies on separate NOT ANY pull-up work. In [P7], the not-null proofs behind NOT IN anti-joins were wrong for quals in JOIN/ON clauses, and the fix was to limit the proofs to WHERE quals. The semantic tests in message #7 cover NULL values and empty subqueries, but not placement in ON clauses or below outer joins.
refuted.author_must_show: Which code proves that a rewritten <> ALL in a JOIN/ON clause or under an outer join keeps NOT IN NULL semantics after pull-up, and which test covers it?

precedents.title: Convert NOT IN to anti-joins when possible

critic.reasoning: The rewrite of `<> ALL` builds the same tree the parser builds for NOT IN, so NULL handling after pull-up belongs to the NOT ANY pull-up code. The proposal shows no wrong result, and [P7] concerned a different patch's not-null proofs.

refuted.title: Negation keeps operator metadata that the new operator may not match
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension defines an operator class whose operators have negators outside the family, as in message #8. After an upgrade, a working ALL query now fails with "operator ... is not a member of opfamily". The user finds out in production, at execution time, and no regression test in core exercised that case.
refuted.argument: The rewrite trusts the NEGATOR declaration but carries over metadata built for the original operator, such as rcexpr->opfamilies. Message #8 shows this breaks a valid operator class that passes amvalidate(). Rui offers three different fixes, and the author has not said which one he accepts. Any metadata later added to RowCompareExpr or to sublink test expressions must also be fixed up in this rewrite, and nothing fails loudly if a future patch misses it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which invariant tells a future patch which fields of the test expression must be rederived after negation, and how would a missed field be caught before release?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The added point about fields that future patches might miss names no concrete field or case.

refuted.title: No way to undo the pull-up when a plan regresses
refuted.failure_scenario: An application with a large reporting query using <> ALL upgrades. The sublink is now pulled up into the outer join problem, which exceeds join_collapse_limit or gains LATERAL limits, and the plan gets slower. The only remedies are raising planner limits for every query or rewriting generated SQL.
refuted.argument: In messages #2 and #5 Lepikhov reports that each new sublink pull-up has produced user complaints, because the parse-tree rewrite is irreversible and has no per-query control. In message #3 the author answers that join search limits are the root cause. That may be true, but the project still handles the reports, and the thread does not settle it. The proposal offers no benchmarks and no off switch, so the cost of any regression falls on the project's support channels.
refuted.author_must_show: What can a user whose ALL query regresses after the pull-up do, short of rewriting the query or raising join_collapse_limit for the whole session?

refuted.title: No field report or measurement shows slow ALL sublinks matter
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer has to weigh a new rewrite in pull-up code that every query with an ALL sublink goes through, and the stated gain rests only on theory. If few real queries use `op ALL`, the project carries the code and the risk of plan changes for a benefit that may never appear in practice.
refuted.argument: The idea comes from reading a paper (message #1), not from a user report of a slow `<> ALL` query. The thread has no -general, -bugs or -performance report and no benchmark numbers. NOT IN is common, but the proposal does not show that users write it as `<> ALL`. [P2] was rejected for this reason: a rewrite for a form users rarely write, with "show any real-world cases where it wins" as the bar.
refuted.author_must_show: Which real workloads or ORMs generate `op ALL` sublinks, and how much faster do they run with v2 on a benchmark?

precedents.title: Pull up sublink of type 'NOT NOT (expr)'

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which makes the same demand point with the more concrete NOT IN equivalence.

refuted.title: Existing ALL queries change plans without asking, and have no opt-out
refuted.failure_scenario: A site with a tuned reporting query that uses `<> ALL` upgrades. The sublink is pulled up into an anti-join, the join list grows past join_collapse_limit, and the query gets a worse plan. The site finds out in production, and its only fixes are raising the limit or rewriting the query.
refuted.argument: Message #2 and message #5 report that new sublink pull-ups often bring user complaints for this reason. Message #3 says the fault lies in the join search, and that does not settle the cost to the users who pay it. The users who pay are the ones with ALL queries that work today. Without measured gains, a committer would likely ask whether those gains outweigh that risk.
refuted.author_must_show: For queries with ALL sublinks, how often does pull-up make plans worse, and what can a user do about it besides raising join_collapse_limit?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. The item 4 framing also fits poorly, because the users who may pay are the same users of ALL sublinks who gain.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The rewrite assumes an operator's negator is in the same opfamily, which user-defined operator classes need not satisfy (message #8).

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Rewrite turns valid row-comparison ALL queries into errors

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: Existing ALL sublinks can become hashed ANY SubPlans, semijoins or anti-joins.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a permanent rewrite in prepjointree.c that must keep operator metadata consistent after negation.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: NOT IN already parses to the tree this patch builds for `<> ALL` and already gets a hashed SubPlan.

questions: Which conditions on negator and opfamily membership does the rewrite require, and does the patch check each one for btree, non-btree and commutated row comparisons?
Which `op ALL` queries run faster with v2, and by how much on a benchmark?
Which real queries, for example from ORMs or query generators, use `op ALL` forms that users cannot write as NOT IN?
What can a user do when a pulled-up ALL sublink gives a worse plan, other than rewrite the query or raise join_collapse_limit?
What does this patch gain alone for `op ALL`, without the pending NOT ANY pull-up patch that message #1 mentions?

committability.owner_note: The maintenance-fit note says the author, Richard Guo, is a planner committer. A second person who knows sublink pull-up and row-comparison opfamilies has not reviewed it in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for plan changes in every existing query with an ALL sublink, and for correct negation with user-defined operators, with no end date.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 in message #6 and kept the entry open across three CommitFests. Message #8 has no reply yet.

priority.reason: The change is confined to prepjointree.c and reuses existing ANY sublink code, so the cost after commit is small. The thread shows no user report or benchmark, and the opfamily error in message #8 needs an answer first.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check that the rewrite keeps NULL semantics in every placement. It also could not check which operator metadata the rewrite rederives after negation.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pulling up direct-correlated ANY_SUBLINK
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner pull up an ANY sublink whose subquery references the immediate outer query level (varlevelsup = 1) by rewriting it as an EXISTS sublink. Today convert_ANY_sublink_to_join gives up on such sublinks, so they run as SubPlans.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane found the patch messy because it duplicated code from elsewhere, and he posted a different approach that drops the contain_vars_of_level restriction and uses LATERAL. Richard Guo showed that without a limit on outer references, LATERAL constraints can leave no legal join order ("failed to build any 3-way joins"). The v2 patch then stopped applying on HEAD, nobody posted a rebased version, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch seems awfully messy to me.  The fact that you're having to
duplicate stuff done elsewhere suggests at the least that you've not
plugged the code into the best place.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pull up sublink of type 'NOT NOT (expr)'
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes any number of consecutive NOTs over a SubLink in pull_up_sublinks, so that quals like "NOT NOT (a.i in (select ...))" or "NOT NOT EXISTS (...)" can be pulled up into joins. Today such SubLinks stay as SubPlans.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that pull_up_sublinks runs before transformations that could create NOT NOT, so it only sees NOT NOT that a user wrote by hand, and no one showed that this happens in real queries. Without such evidence the extra code and planning cycles would be a net loss for everyone else. Running expression simplification before pullup would need a second simplification pass, which he judged not worth the cost. The author agreed and asked for the patch to be rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So I'm inclined to reject this patch as probably being a net loss in
almost all cases.  If you can show any real-world cases where it wins,
we could reconsider.

precedents_retrieved.title: allow partial union-all and improve parallel subquery costing
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner build partial paths for UNION ALL so the branches can run under a parallel plan. It also changes subquery costing to account for parallelism, with a regression test and before/after plans for TPC-DS query 5.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took up the patch during the commitfests. In March 2021 the patch no longer applied, and the entry was set to Waiting for Author. The author sent no rebased patch, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since no new patch has been provided, marking this Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: NOT IN to ANTI JOIN transformation
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch rewrites NOT IN (subquery) into an anti join when the subquery is not eligible for a hashed subplan. It handles nullable columns by adding OR ... IS NULL terms to the join condition and a filter on the outer side, and adds a routine that proves column non-nullability.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown message is a rebased patch from June 2019, and no later reply appears before the April 2020 decision. Earlier, David Rowley noted that the added OR ... IS NULL join clauses force a nested loop join, and moved his competing patch to a separate thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: add explicit partial union-all and improve parallel subquery costing
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner build partial Append paths for UNION ALL subqueries so their branches can run in parallel. It also changes subquery scan costing to take parallel workers into account in the row estimate.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding after Ronan Dunklau's review asked for a regression test of the new partial append path and questioned the subquery scan row estimate change. Daniel Gustafsson closed the entry because the thread stalled with these requests unanswered. An earlier round was also closed after the patch needed a rebase and no new version came in time.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
With the thread stalled and requests for a test (documentation really?) not
responded to I'm marking this patch Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Memoize ANTI and SEMI JOIN inner
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner put a Memoize node on the parameterized inner side of a Nested Loop semi join or anti join, so pulled-up EXISTS and NOT EXISTS sublinks can reuse cached inner results. It relies on Memoize single-row mode, because each outer row needs only the first inner match.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Richard Guo showed that the change is unsafe for semi and anti joins unless the inner side is provably unique. Join clauses from an upper level can move to the semi join, so a second inner tuple arrives and fails with "cache entry already complete". A semi join with a provably unique inner is already reduced to an inner join, so the work narrowed to proving inner_unique for anti joins, and Richard Guo posted a patch for that. The visible messages do not show why the entry was then withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I conducted some experiments, and I'm afraid it's not safe to consider Memoize for semi or anti joins, unless the inner side is provably unique.

precedents_retrieved.title: Convert NOT IN to anti-joins when possible
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the planner convert a NOT IN subquery into an anti-join when it can prove that neither the subquery output nor the outer expression can be NULL. The planner would do this without costing, as it already does for NOT EXISTS.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Antonin Houska showed that join quals used as not-null proofs can be wrong when the NOT IN is in a JOIN/ON clause, because join order may let NULLs reach the anti-join. David Rowley limited the optimisation to WHERE-clause quals, and Antonin then sent review comments on that version. The author said he had no time to respond, and the entry was returned with feedback after about three months with no update.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It has been close to three months since this last update, so marked
the patch as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Protect syscache from bloating with negative cache entries
precedents_retrieved.summary: The first patches removed negative catcache entries through invalidation callbacks, for example when a relation or a schema is dropped. The later version adds a GUC, catalog_cache_prune_min_age, so that a backend removes catcache entries not accessed for that long when it would otherwise grow the hash table.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. In the last technical messages, from January 2021, Heikki Linnakangas found the slowdown acceptable and suggested enabling the feature by default. Bruce Momjian asked in March 2021 whether it would make PG 14, and no later message is shown.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
Reverted commit(s): Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2aa6e33, that added a fast path to skip
anti-wraparound and non-aggressive autovacuum jobs (these have no sense
as anti-wraparound implies aggressive).  With a cluster using a high
amount of relations with a portion of them being heavily updated, this
could cause autovacuum to lock down, with autovacuum workers attempting
repeatedly those jobs on the same relations for the same database, that
just kept being skipped.  This lock down can be solved with a manual
VACUUM FREEZE.

Justin King has reported one environment where the issue happened, and
Julien Rouhaud and I have been able to reproduce it in a second
environment.  With a very aggressive autovacuum_freeze_max_age,
triggering those jobs with pgbench is a matter of minutes, and hitting
the lock down is a lot harder (my local tests failed to do that).

Note that anti-wraparound and non-aggressive jobs can only be triggered
on a subset of shared catalogs:
- pg_auth_members
- pg_authid
- pg_database
- pg_replication_origin
- pg_shseclabel
- pg_subscription
- pg_tablespace
While the lock down was possible down to v12, the root cause of those
jobs is a much older issue, which needs more analysis.

Bonus thanks to Andres Freund for the discussion.

roaster_notes.note: [P1] was skipped. Its LATERAL and code-duplication problems came from pulling up correlated ANY sublinks, and this patch reuses the existing ANY pull-up rules unchanged.
The De Morgan rewrite itself keeps SQL three-valued semantics, and negate_clause() already uses negators to flip ANY and ALL for array expressions, so trusting negators follows existing practice.

The patch changes only planner prep code in prepjointree.c and regression tests, so it adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, wire-protocol or ABI state. Stored views and rules keep the original ALL sublink in their parse trees because the rewrite happens at plan time, so pg_dump and pg_upgrade are unaffected.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect that is new. It rewrites an ALL sublink into a negated ANY sublink by swapping each operator for its declared negator. The planner already trusts NEGATOR the same way when it simplifies NOT (a < b) into a >= b. EXECUTE on the negator's function is still checked at run time, so a missing grant gives an error and no escalation. After pull-up, the existing leakproof and security barrier rules for quals still apply. A user-defined operator whose NEGATOR does not match its meaning gives wrong results only to queries that use that operator, as it does today. The opfamily error in message #8 is a correctness problem, outside this angle.

Fit is good otherwise. The author is a planner committer, the change is confined to prepjointree.c, and it reuses existing ANY sublink machinery. The cost for queries without ALL sublinks appears negligible, unlike the planning-cycle concern in [P2].
No extension or hook covers this rewrite. A planner rewrite of this kind belongs in core, so the only objection from this angle concerns demand beyond the NOT IN spelling.
The demand case is thin, not absent, so both objections are "not now, show demand". A few real cases with numbers would settle them.
